claim: Bile is an important component of the human gastrointestinal tract with an essential role in food absorption and antimicrobial activities.
source: Bile is an important component of the human gastrointestinal tract with an essential role in food absorption and antimicrobial activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Begley et al., 2005, which provides external scholarly support for the statement.

claim: The main components of bile are bile salts, cholesterol, and phospholipids that together possess antimicrobial activities.
source: Its main components are bile salts, cholesterol, and phospholipids that together possess antimicrobial activities, challenging the survival and colonization of both pathogenic and commensal bacteria (Begley et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Begley et al., 2005.

claim: Enteric bacterial pathogens can utilize bile as a signaling cue to regulate gene expression profiles during host infection.
source: There is increasing evidence that enteric bacterial pathogens can utilize bile as a signaling cue to regulate gene expression profiles during host infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples and citations in the text.

claim: Salmonella typhimurium senses bile to repress genes involved in invasion when growing in the intestinal lumen.
source: For example, Salmonella typhimurium senses bile to repress the genes involved in invasion when growing in the intestinal lumen and induce their expression to promote invasion upon the penetration of the mucosal layer wherein the concentration of bile is decreased (Prouty and Gunn, 2000; Prouty et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Prouty and Gunn, 2000 and Prouty et al., 2004.

claim: In Shigella spp., bile salts increase the pathogen's adherence and invasion of epithelial cells.
source: In Shigella spp., bile salts increase the pathogen's adherence and invasion of epithelial cells (Pope et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pope et al., 1995.

claim: V. cholerae produces two major virulence factors during infection: cholera toxin (CT) and toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP).
source: V. cholerae produces two major virulence factors during infection, cholera toxin (CT) and toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), and these factors are repressed by ToxT in the presence of bile (Gupta and Chowdhury, 1997; Schuhmacher and Klose, 1999; Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Faruque et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CT and TCP are repressed by ToxT in the presence of bile.
source: V. cholerae produces two major virulence factors during infection, cholera toxin (CT) and toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), and these factors are repressed by ToxT in the presence of bile (Gupta and Chowdhury, 1997; Schuhmacher and Klose, 1999; Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Faruque et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gupta and Chowdhury, 1997; Schuhmacher and Klose, 1999; Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Faruque et al., 1998.

claim: Bile can activate the production of CT independent of ToxT.
source: However, it was also reported that bile can activate the production of CT independent of ToxT (Hung and Mekalanos, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hung and Mekalanos, 2005.

claim: Non-O1/non-O139 V. cholerae strains that do not encode CT and TCP can cause gastroenteritis and utilize bile to activate a pathogenic type III secretion system.
source: Non-O1/non-O139 V. cholerae strains that do not encode CT and TCP can cause gastroenteritis and utilize bile to activate a pathogenic type III secretion system (Dziejman et al., 2005; Chaand et al., 2015; Alam et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dziejman et al., 2005; Chaand et al., 2015; Alam et al., 2010.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus type III secretion system 2 (T3SS2) is induced specifically by bile salts during infection, resulting in acute gastroenteritis.
source: Similarly, V. parahaemolyticus type III secretion system 2 (T3SS2) is induced specifically by bile salts during infection, resulting in acute gastroenteritis (Gotoh et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gotoh et al., 2010.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus is a globally-spread, Gram-negative, halophilic bacterial pathogen that inhabits marine and estuarine environments.
source: V. parahaemolyticus is a globally-spread, Gram-negative, halophilic bacterial pathogen that inhabits marine and estuarine environments and is the world's leading cause of acute gastroenteritis due to the consumption of raw or undercooked seafood (Broberg et al., 2011; Zhang and Orth, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broberg et al., 2011 and Zhang and Orth, 2013.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus is the world's leading cause of acute gastroenteritis due to the consumption of raw or undercooked seafood.
source: V. parahaemolyticus is a globally-spread, Gram-negative, halophilic bacterial pathogen that inhabits marine and estuarine environments and is the world's leading cause of acute gastroenteritis due to the consumption of raw or undercooked seafood (Broberg et al., 2011; Zhang and Orth, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broberg et al., 2011 and Zhang and Orth, 2013.

claim: Rising temperatures in the ocean have contributed to V. parahaemolyticus's worldwide dissemination.
source: During recent years, rising temperatures in the ocean has contributed to this pathogen's worldwide dissemination (Nair et al., 2007; Velazquez-Roman et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2005; O'Boyle and Boyd, 2014; Daniels et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus is the causative agent of the devastating shrimp disease Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis Disease (AHPND).
source: V. parahaemolyticus is also the causative agent of the devastating shrimp disease Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis Disease (AHPND) (Tran et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tran et al., 2013 and Lee et al., 2015.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus encodes two T3SSs: the cytotoxic T3SS1 and the enterotoxic T3SS2.
source: As part of its virulence repertoire, V. parahaemolyticus encodes two T3SSs: the cytotoxic T3SS1 and the enterotoxic T3SS2.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and subsequent citations.

claim: T3SSs encode needle-like secretion apparatuses used to deliver bacterial effector proteins, called Vops, which allow V. parahaemolyticus to invade and kill infected host cells.
source: T3SSs encode needle-like secretion apparatuses used to deliver bacterial effector proteins, called Vops, which allow V. parahaemolyticus to invade and kill infected host cells (Broberg et al., 2011; Makino et al., 2003; Galán and Wolf-Watz, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broberg et al., 2011; Makino et al., 2003; Galán and Wolf-Watz, 2006.

claim: The T3SS1 exclusively secretes VopQ, VopR, VPA0450 and VopS.
source: For example, the T3SS1 exclusively secretes VopQ, VopR, VPA0450 and VopS and uses the effectors to orchestrate a multifaceted host cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: T3SS1 is found in all strains of V. parahaemolyticus.
source: This system is found in all strains of V. parahaemolyticus, and therefore is proposed to be important for bacterial survival in the environment (Broberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Broberg et al., 2011.

claim: T3SS2 is present in clinical isolates of V. parahaemolyticus.
source: T3SS2 is present in clinical isolates of V. parahaemolyticus and is a key bile salt-induced virulence system that causes enterotoxicity and symptoms associated with gastroenteritis during infection (Broberg et al., 2011; Park et al., 2004; Hiyoshi et al., 2010; Ritchie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: T3SS2 is a key bile salt-induced virulence system that causes enterotoxicity and symptoms associated with gastroenteritis during infection.
source: T3SS2 is present in clinical isolates of V. parahaemolyticus and is a key bile salt-induced virulence system that causes enterotoxicity and symptoms associated with gastroenteritis during infection (Broberg et al., 2011; Park et al., 2004; Hiyoshi et al., 2010; Ritchie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broberg et al., 2011; Park et al., 2004; Hiyoshi et al., 2010; Ritchie et al., 2012.

claim: Bile salts induce Vops, such as VopA and VopC, and the needle-like secretion apparatus, including components such as T3SS2 translocon VopD2.
source: Bile salts not only induce Vops, such as VopA and VopC, but also the needle-like secretion apparatus, including components such as T3SS2 translocon VopD2 (Broberg et al., 2011; Zhang and Orth, 2013; Trosky et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broberg et al., 2011; Zhang and Orth, 2013; Trosky et al., 2004.

claim: The activation of T3SS2 by bile salts is regulated by two transmembrane ToxR-like transcription factors, VtrA (VPA1332) and VtrB (VPA1348).
source: In V. parahaemolyticus, the activation of T3SS2 by bile salts is regulated by two transmembrane ToxR-like transcription factors, VtrA (VPA1332) and VtrB (VPA1348) (Gotoh et al., 2010; Kodama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gotoh et al., 2010 and Kodama et al., 2010.

claim: Homologues of VtrA and VtrB, named VttRA and VttRB respectively, have been identified in T3SS-containing non-O1/non-O139 V. cholerae strains and function in a similar way.
source: Homologues of VtrA and VtrB, named VttRA and VttRB respectively, have been identified in T3SS-containing non-O1/non-O139 V. cholerae strains and function in a similar way (Alam et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alam et al., 2010.

claim: VtrC (VPA1333) from V. parahaemolyticus is a previously unrecognized component necessary for bile salt sensing and T3SS2 activation.
source: Here, we identify VtrC (VPA1333) from V. parahaemolyticus as a previously unrecognized component necessary for bile salt sensing and T3SS2 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: vtrC is constitutively co-transcribed with vtrA as an overlapping 3' open reading frame.
source: vtrC is constitutively co-transcribed with vtrA as an overlapping 3' open reading frame.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The periplasmic domains of the transmembrane proteins, VtrA and VtrC, form a functional complex that binds bile salts.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the periplasmic domains of the transmembrane proteins, VtrA and VtrC, form a functional complex that binds bile salts to activate VtrA's cytoplasmic DNA binding domain, which in turn induces T3SS2 via the downstream transcription factor VtrB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation, ITC, and structural analysis.

claim: The VtrA/VtrC complex activates VtrA's cytoplasmic DNA binding domain upon binding bile salts.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the periplasmic domains of the transmembrane proteins, VtrA and VtrC, form a functional complex that binds bile salts to activate VtrA's cytoplasmic DNA binding domain, which in turn induces T3SS2 via the downstream transcription factor VtrB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: The structure of VtrA/VtrC periplasmic domains reveals an obligate heterodimer where VtrC recruits structural elements from VtrA to complete a β-barrel with a hydrophobic inner chamber that binds bile salts.
source: The structure of VtrA/VtrC periplasmic domains reveals an obligate heterodimer where VtrC recruits structural elements from VtrA to complete a β-barrel with a hydrophobic inner chamber that binds bile salts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A co-crystal structure of the VtrA/VtrC heterodimer with a bile salt reveals that ligand binding occurs in the hydrophobic inner chamber of VtrC.
source: A co-crystal structure of the VtrA/VtrC heterodimer with a bile salt reveals that ligand binding occurs in the hydrophobic inner chamber of VtrC, similar to that found for the family of monomeric calycins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Mutations of residues within the hydrophobic chamber that are important for bile salt-binding disrupt bile salt activation of T3SS2.
source: Mutations of residues within the hydrophobic chamber that are important for bile salt-binding disrupt bile salt activation of T3SS2.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis data presented in Figure 9.

claim: vtrC is located directly downstream of vtrA.
source: vtrC (vpa1333) is a previously uncharacterized gene in V. parahaemolyticus that is located directly downstream of vtrA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text and Figure 1A showing the gene organization.

claim: The open reading frames for vtrA and vtrC overlap by 17 nucleotides.
source: The open reading frames for vtrA and vtrC overlap by 17 nucleotides, suggesting that they are likely in the same operon and function in the same biological process.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis.

claim: The gene organization of vtrA, vtrC and vtrB in the genome is highly conserved in other Vibrio and related species.
source: We observed that the gene organization of vtrA, vtrC and vtrB in the genome is highly conserved in other Vibrio and related species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: V. cholerae non-O1/O139 strains and Grimontia hollisae possess a T3SS similar to T3SS2 in V. parahaemolyticus and cause gastroenteritis during human infection.
source: Both V. cholerae non-O1/O139 strains and Grimontia hollisae possess a T3SS similar to T3SS2 in V. parahaemolyticus and cause gastroenteritis during human infection (Dziejman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dziejman et al., 2005.

claim: vtrA and vtrC are co-transcribed before and after bile salt-mediated T3SS2 induction.
source: RT-PCR of the region spanning vtrA and vtrC showed that these genes are indeed in the same operon and co-transcribed before and after bile salt-mediated T3SS2 induction (Figure 1B, lanes 3, 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VtrC is conserved in various Vibrio and related species, as well as in Moritella.
source: PSI-BLAST analysis with the predicted VtrC protein sequence revealed that it is conserved in various Vibrio and related species, as well as in Moritella.
evidence: This claim is supported by PSI-BLAST bioinformatics analysis.

claim: VtrC has a highly conserved N-terminal transmembrane signal anchor that is predicted to direct and retain proteins in the bacterial membrane.
source: VtrC has a highly conserved N-terminal transmembrane signal anchor that is predicted to direct and retain proteins in the bacterial membrane (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and prediction algorithms, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ten other strains of bacteria contain homologous genes of vtrA and vtrC but not vtrB.
source: Furthermore, ten other strains of bacteria contain homologous genes of vtrA and vtrC but not vtrB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: VtrA and VtrC evolved independently of VtrB.
source: These results support the hypothesis that VtrA and VtrC evolved independently of VtrB.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bioinformatics data showing that some bacteria have vtrA and vtrC but not vtrB.

claim: Deletion of vtrC completely abolished the activation of T3SS2 by bile salts.
source: Deletion of vtrC completely abolished the activation of T3SS2 by bile salts, as shown by the loss of expression and secretion of the T3SS2 effectors VopA and VopC, and of the T3SS2 translocon VopD2 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Complementation of vtrC deletion by a vector expressing VtrC fully restored the activity of T3SS2.
source: Complementation of vtrC deletion by a vector expressing VtrC fully restored the activity of T3SS2 (Figure 2A,B), indicating that the phenotypes observed in the vtrC deletion were not caused by a polar effect on neighboring genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The effect of VtrC is specific to T3SS2 because its deletion had no impact on the expression and secretion of the T3SS1 effector VopS.
source: The effect of VtrC is specific to T3SS2 because its deletion had no impact on the expression and secretion of the T3SS1 effector VopS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VtrC is required for T3SS2 activation by bile salts.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that VtrC is required for T3SS2 activation by bile salts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that deletion of vtrC abolishes T3SS2 activation.

claim: VtrC is an inner membrane protein with the N-terminal 1–9 amino acids facing the cytoplasm, a single transmembrane helix (10–24 amino acids) and the C-terminal domain (25–161 amino acids) in the periplasm.
source: Analysis of the VtrC protein sequence using membrane topology prediction programs, TMpred, TMHMM 2.0, HMMtop 2.0, and Phobius indicates VtrC is an inner membrane protein with the N-terminal 1–9 amino acids facing the cytoplasm, a single transmembrane helix (10–24 amino acids) and the C-terminal domain (25–161 amino acids) in the periplasm (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions and experimental validation using PhoA and LacZ reporter assays.

claim: PhoA is active only in the periplasm after disulfide bond formation and dimerization.
source: PhoA is active only in the periplasm after disulfide bond formation and dimerization, whereas LacZ only exhibits enzymatic activity in the cytoplasm where it can fold properly (van Geest and Lolkema, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Geest and Lolkema, 2000.

claim: LacZ only exhibits enzymatic activity in the cytoplasm where it can fold properly.
source: PhoA is active only in the periplasm after disulfide bond formation and dimerization, whereas LacZ only exhibits enzymatic activity in the cytoplasm where it can fold properly (van Geest and Lolkema, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Geest and Lolkema, 2000.

claim: PhoA was active when fused to the C-terminus of VtrC, but not N-terminus.
source: As expected, PhoA was active when fused to the C-terminus of VtrC, but not N-terminus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PhoA activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LacZ was more active when fused to the N-terminus of VtrC.
source: In addition, LacZ was more active when fused to the N-terminus of VtrC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by LacZ activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: VtrC is localized to the inner membrane with the N-terminal 9 amino acids in the cytoplasm and the C-terminal domain in the periplasm.
source: These observations demonstrate that VtrC is localized to the inner membrane with the N-terminal 9 amino acids in the cytoplasm and the C-terminal domain in the periplasm.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PhoA and LacZ reporter assay data.

claim: VtrA directly controls the expression of VtrB.
source: Previous studies have shown that VtrA directly controls the expression of VtrB and that both proteins are inner membrane proteins with their N-terminal DNA binding domain oriented in the cytoplasm and their C-terminal region in the periplasm (Figure 4A) (Kodama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kodama et al., 2010.

claim: VtrA and VtrB are inner membrane proteins with their N-terminal DNA binding domain oriented in the cytoplasm and their C-terminal region in the periplasm.
source: Previous studies have shown that VtrA directly controls the expression of VtrB and that both proteins are inner membrane proteins with their N-terminal DNA binding domain oriented in the cytoplasm and their C-terminal region in the periplasm (Figure 4A) (Kodama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kodama et al., 2010.

claim: VtrC functions upstream of VtrB.
source: Thus, VtrC appears to function upstream of VtrB via a signaling cascade including VtrA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that deletion of vtrC prevents induction of vtrB.

claim: The deletion of vtrC did not change the mRNA level of VtrA.
source: The deletion of vtrC did not change the mRNA level of VtrA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of vtrC resulted in decreased protein levels of VtrA independent of bile salts.
source: Interestingly, deletion of vtrC resulted in decreased protein levels of VtrA independent of bile salts (Figure 4C, lanes 3 and 7), suggesting that the presence of VtrC might stabilize VtrA.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of VtrC might stabilize VtrA.
source: Interestingly, deletion of vtrC resulted in decreased protein levels of VtrA independent of bile salts (Figure 4C, lanes 3 and 7), suggesting that the presence of VtrC might stabilize VtrA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VtrA protein levels decrease when vtrC is deleted.

claim: Ectopic expression of VtrC from a plasmid rescued VtrA levels.
source: Ectopic expression of VtrC from a plasmid rescued VtrA levels (Figure 4C, lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The absence of VtrC prevented the induction of vtrB upon T3SS2 activation with bile salts.
source: As was previously observed for VtrA, the absence of VtrC prevented the induction of vtrB upon T3SS2 activation with bile salts (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Endogenous VtrA co-precipitated with VtrC, indicating that these two proteins interact in vivo.
source: Analysis of FLAG immunoprecipitates revealed that endogenous VtrA co-precipitated with VtrC, indicating that these two proteins interact in vivo (Figure 5A, lanes 3 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: VtrA and VtrC interact in the presence and absence of bile salts.
source: VtrA and VtrC interact in the presence and absence of bile salts, suggesting that these proteins interact independently of bile salts before activation of T3SS2 by bile salts, and remain in a complex after treatment with bile salts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The VtrA/VtrC complex eluted as a 29.5 kDa species by SEC, indicating a 1:1 heterodimer of VtrA (11.0 kDa) and VtrC (16.9 kDa) periplasmic domains.
source: The VtrA/VtrC complex eluted as a 29.5 kDa species by SEC, indicating a 1:1 heterodimer of VtrA (11.0 kDa) and VtrC (16.9 kDa) periplasmic domains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VtrA alone appeared to elute as a monomer of approximately 11 kDa.
source: VtrA alone appeared to elute as a monomer of approximately 11 kDa (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The VtrA and VtrC subunits in the heterodimer make extensive interactions with each other, with an interface area of 1,149 Å2.
source: The VtrA and VtrC subunits in the heterodimer make extensive interactions with each other (Figure 6B), with an interface area of 1,149 Å2 (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The VtrA/VtrC heterodimer is the only stable quaternary structure in solution.
source: An analysis of the macromolecular interfaces in this crystalline lattice by the web server PDBePISA (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/pisa/pistart.html) (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) indicate that the VtrA/VtrC heterodimer is the only stable quaternary structure in solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using PDBePISA.

claim: The VtrC subunit consists of eight β-strands and a short α-helix.
source: The VtrC subunit consists of eight β-strands and a short α-helix.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The eight β-strands of VtrC form a β-sheet meander that folds into itself to form a β-barrel with a small space between the first and last β-strands (Aβ and Iβ).
source: The eight β-strands of VtrC form a β-sheet meander that folds into itself to form a β-barrel with a small space between the first and last β-strands (Aβ and Iβ) (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data and Video 1.

claim: The β-barrel is lined on the inside by hydrophobic side chains.
source: The β-barrel is lined on the inside by hydrophobic side chains (Figure 6C) and is covered on one side by the short α-helix (Fα) and an adjacent disordered loop, which could not be modeled in its entirety due to the poor electron density of this region (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: VtrC shares structural similarity with lipocalins, fatty acid binding proteins (FABPs), avidins, metalloprotease inhibitors (MPIs), and other members of the calycin superfamily of proteins.
source: Despite the lack of sequence similarity to proteins of known function, VtrC shares structural similarity with lipocalins, fatty acid binding proteins (FABPs), avidins, metalloprotease inhibitors (MPIs), and other members of the calycin superfamily of proteins (Figure 7) (Flower et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 7 and citation to Flower et al., 2000.

claim: The inside of the calycin β-barrel often acts as a binding site for fatty acids and other hydrophobic molecules, such as retinol and biotin.
source: The inside of the calycin β-barrel often acts as a binding site for fatty acids and other hydrophobic molecules, such as retinol and biotin (Flower et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Flower et al., 2000.

claim: VtrC adopts a new fold within the calycin superfamily.
source: Comparison of the overall VtrC structure with other calycins suggests that it adopts a new fold within the superfamily.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural comparison analysis.

claim: VtrA/VtrC would be the first member of the calycin family that is an obligate dimer and not only binds a hydrophobic ligand but also transmits a signal upon binding.
source: Interestingly, VtrA/VtrC would be the first member of this family that is an obligate dimer and not only binds a hydrophobic ligand but also transmits a signal upon binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural and functional characterization of VtrA/VtrC.

claim: The VtrA subunit adopts an alpha/beta fold with a five-stranded β-sheet and two α-helices on one side of the sheet.
source: The VtrA subunit adopts an alpha/beta fold with a five-stranded β-sheet and two α-helices on one side of the sheet (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: VtrA Fβ intercalates between VtrC Aβ and Iβ, making numerous polar contacts with VtrC Aβ and closing the gap in the VtrC β-barrel.
source: VtrA Fβ intercalates between VtrC Aβ and Iβ, making numerous polar contacts with VtrC Aβ and closing the gap in the VtrC β-barrel (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The incorporation of structural elements from VtrA into the β-barrel fold suggests that VtrC may not fold properly in isolation.
source: The incorporation of structural elements from VtrA into the β-barrel fold suggests that VtrC may not fold properly in isolation and is consistent with our inability to purify the VtrC periplasmic domain in the absence of VtrA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural data and experimental observations.

claim: Taurodeoxycholate (TDC) and glycodeoxycholate (GDC), but not chenodeoxycholate (CDC) or cholate (CA), could activate the V. parahaemolyticus T3SS2.
source: We validated that taurodeoxycholate (TDC) and glycodeoxycholate (GDC), but not chenodeoxycholate (CDC) or cholate (CA), could activate the V. parahaemolyticus T3SS2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TDC binds to the VtrA/VtrC heterodimer in an exothermic manner with a dissociation constant (KD) of 315.4 nM.
source: These results indicated that TDC binds to the VtrA/VtrC heterodimer in an exothermic manner (Figure 8), with a dissociation constant (KD) of 315.4 nM (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The stoichiometry of TDC binding to VtrA/VtrC is approximately 1:1 (n = 0.94).
source: The stoichiometry of TDC binding to VtrA/VtrC is approximately 1:1 (n = 0.94).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: VtrA and VtrC form a functional complex that can bind bile salts.
source: Taken together our results suggest that VtrA and VtrC form a functional complex that can bind bile salts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ITC and structural data.

claim: The model contains three VtrA/VtrC heterodimers in the asymmetric unit, each with clear electron density for one TDC molecule bound inside the β-barrel.
source: The model reveals three VtrA/VtrC heterodimers in the asymmetric unit, each with clear electron density for one TDC molecule bound inside the β-barrel (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A fourth TDC molecule mediated lattice contacts between VtrA chain A and its symmetry mate.
source: A fourth TDC molecule mediated lattice contacts between VtrA chain A and its symmetry mate (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The largest differences between the VtrA/VtrC-TDC and the apo heterodimers are in the VtrC disordered loop and Fα that follows it.
source: The largest differences between the VtrA/VtrC-TDC and the apo heterodimers are in the VtrC disordered loop and Fα that follows it.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the VtrA/VtrC-TDC heterodimer, the disordered loop has been displaced by the TDC molecule and is now observable in two out of the three heterodimers in the crystallographic asymmetric unit.
source: In the VtrA/VtrC-TDC heterodimer, the disordered loop has been displaced by the TDC molecule and is now observable in two out of the three heterodimers in the crystallographic asymmetric unit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data.

claim: Ser123 forms a hydrogen bond with the 12α-hydroxyl group of TDC.
source: Remarkably, one of these residues (Ser123) now forms a hydrogen bond with the 12α-hydroxyl group of TDC (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The main chain amide between F150 and Tyr151 (Hβ-Iβ loop) coordinates the 3α-hydroxyl group.
source: The main chain amide between F150 and Tyr151 (Hβ-Iβ loop) coordinates the 3α-hydroxyl group (Figure 8C), which is present in all bile salts, suggesting that this interaction is important for specificity towards bile salts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The interaction between the main chain amide between F150 and Tyr151 and the 3α-hydroxyl group is important for specificity towards bile salts.
source: The main chain amide between F150 and Tyr151 (Hβ-Iβ loop) coordinates the 3α-hydroxyl group (Figure 8C), which is present in all bile salts, suggesting that this interaction is important for specificity towards bile salts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural observation that the 3α-hydroxyl group is present in all bile salts.

claim: Several VtrC residues in the binding pocket maintain hydrophobic interactions with TDC, including the side chains of Phe150 with steroid ring A and Tyr81 with the hydrophobic part of the bile acid.
source: Several VtrC residues in the binding pocket maintain hydrophobic interactions with TDC, including the side chains of Phe150 with steroid ring A and Tyr81 with the hydrophobic part of the bile acid (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The mutation of His50 to an arginine residue is expected to produce steric hindrance by insertion of a large side chain into the bile salt binding pocket.
source: The mutation of His50, located at the top of the hydrophobic cleft, to an arginine residue is expected to produce steric hindrance by insertion of a large side chain into the bile salt binding pocket (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural analysis and the properties of the amino acid substitution.

claim: When VtrC-H50R was expressed in the vtrC deletion strain and bile salts were added, the T3SS2 could not be induced.
source: When VtrC-H50R was expressed in the vtrC deletion strain and bile salts were added, the T3SS2 could not be induced as indicated by the lack of expression and secretion of the T3SS2 effector VopA (Figure 9B, lanes 5 and 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Changing Tyr81 to an alanine residue would disrupt bile salt binding by eliminating the interaction between the Tyr81 aromatic ring and the bile salt side chain.
source: We also changed Tyr81 to an alanine residue, which we predicted would disrupt bile salt binding by eliminating the interaction between the Tyr81 aromatic ring and the bile salt side chain (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural analysis and the properties of the amino acid substitution.

claim: When VtrC-Y81A was expressed in the vtrC deletion strain and bile salts were added, the T3SS2 was not induced.
source: When VtrC-Y81A was expressed in the vtrC deletion strain and bile salts were added, the T3SS2 was not induced as indicated by the lack of expression and secretion of VopA (Figure 9B, lanes 6 and 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The VtrC-Q42A mutant rescued the vtrC deletion strain and upon addition of bile salts the T3SS2 was activated.
source: As expected, this mutant rescued the vtrC deletion strain and upon addition of bile salts the T3SS2 was activated as indicated by the expression and secretion of VopA (Figure 9B, lanes 4 and 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The wild type and mutant VtrC proteins formed a stable complex with endogenous VtrA, as indicated by their co-immunopreciptation.
source: As seen in Figure 9C, the wild type and mutant VtrC proteins formed a stable complex with endogenous VtrA, as indicated by their co-immunopreciptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Bile sensing plays a significant role in human infection caused by various enteric bacterial pathogens.
source: Bile sensing plays a significant role in human infection caused by various enteric bacterial pathogens (Begley et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Begley et al., 2005.

claim: Bile salt-induced T3SSs are the primary virulence factor in many Vibrio species.
source: Bile salt-induced T3SSs are the primary virulence factor in many Vibrio species (Broberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Broberg et al., 2011.

claim: The periplasmic domains of the inner membrane proteins VtrA and VtrC form a stable complex that functions as a receptor for bile salts.
source: Our biochemical data and the structural analysis demonstrated that the periplasmic domains of the inner membrane proteins VtrA and VtrC form a stable complex that functions as a receptor for bile salts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of the VtrA/VtrC complex reveals that their periplasmic domains form a obligate heterodimer where VtrC folds into an open eight-stranded β-barrel and VtrA adopts a mixed α/β structure whereby one of its a β-strands contributes to the formation of the β-barrel.
source: The crystal structure of the VtrA/VtrC complex reveals that their periplasmic domains form a obligate heterodimer where VtrC folds into an open eight-stranded β-barrel and VtrA adopts a mixed α/β structure whereby one of its a β-strands contributes to the formation of the β-barrel.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The VtrA/VtrC heterodimer fold is similar to members of the calycin superfamily, which contain eight to ten-stranded β-barrels that often bind hydrophobic molecules.
source: The VtrA/VtrC heterodimer fold is similar to members of the calycin superfamily, which contain eight to ten-stranded β-barrels that often bind hydrophobic molecules (Flower et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citation to Flower et al., 2000.

claim: Calycins have low sequence similarity, but relatively high structural conservation.
source: Calycins have low sequence similarity, but relatively high structural conservation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the calycin superfamily.

claim: VtrC does not seem to cluster with any particular calycin family and it forms its own clade.
source: In terms of structure, VtrC does not seem to cluster with any particular family and it forms its own clade (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Members of the FABP family have been found to bind bile salts.
source: Interestingly, members of the FABP family have been found to bind bile salts.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples and citations.

claim: Human and porcine ileal lipid binding proteins (ILBPs) bind bile salts.
source: This is exemplified by human and porcine ileal lipid binding proteins (ILBPs), and their NMR structures in complex with taurocholate (Kurz et al., 2003) and glycocholate (Lücke et al., 2000), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kurz et al., 2003 and Lücke et al., 2000.

claim: FABPs have a helix-turn-helix motif that forms a lid over one side of the barrel and is proposed to act as a portal for ligand access.
source: Analogous to VtrC's disordered loop and short α-helix, FABPs have a helix-turn-helix motif that forms a lid over one side of the barrel and is proposed to act as a portal for ligand access (Storch and McDermott, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Storch and McDermott, 2009.

claim: Ligand binding in FABPs induces subtle conformational changes that promote protein-membrane or protein-protein interactions.
source: In the case of FABPs, it has been suggested that ligand binding induces subtle conformational changes that promote protein-membrane or protein-protein interactions (Storch and McDermott, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Storch and McDermott, 2009.

claim: Upon binding bile salt, an unstructured loop in VtrA/VtrC is translocated from the inside of the hydrophobic chamber to the outside of the chamber, where it becomes structured.
source: We observe a similar scenario for the VtrA/VtrC obligate heterodimer bound to bile salts where, upon binding bile salt, it appears an unstructured loop is translocated from the inside of the hydrophobic chamber to the outside of the chamber, where it becomes structured.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the apo and TDC-bound crystal structures.

claim: The GrlR/GrlA complex is a regulator of the T3SS-encoding locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) in enterohaemorrhagic and enteropathogenic E. coli strains (EHEC and EPEC, respectively).
source: The closest example with regard to complex formation and function is the GrlR/GrlA complex, a regulator of the T3SS-encoding locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) in enterohaemorrhagic and enteropathogenic E. coli strains (EHEC and EPEC, respectively) (Padavannil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Padavannil et al., 2013.

claim: GrlR is a cytosolic lipocalin that represses the LEE repressor GrlA by binding to its helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain.
source: GrlR is a cytosolic lipocalin that represses the LEE repressor GrlA by binding to its helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the GrlR/GrlA system.

claim: grlR and grlA are transcribed from a bicistronic operon.
source: Similar to vtrA and vtrC, grlR and grlA are transcribed from a bicistronic operon, although the order of the lipocalin and transcriptional regulator genes is reversed in the latter pair.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the GrlR/GrlA system.

claim: The structure of GrlR in complex with the GrlA HTH domain revealed a heterotrimeric complex where a GrlR dimer binds one GrlA HTH monomer.
source: Analytical ultracentrifugation and the structure of GrlR in complex with the GrlA HTH domain revealed a heterotrimeric complex where a GrlR dimer binds one GrlA HTH monomer (PDB ID: 4KT5) (Padavannil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Padavannil et al., 2013.

claim: The inner cavity of GrlR binds lipids.
source: It has been shown that the inner cavity of GrlR binds lipids (Jobichen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jobichen et al., 2009.

claim: The genes encoding ToxR/ToxS and TcpP/TcpH are arranged in bicistronic operons.
source: First, the genes encoding the proteins in each pair are arranged in bicistronic operons (Miller et al., 1989; Häse and Mekalanos, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1989 and Häse and Mekalanos, 1998.

claim: VtrA/ToxR/TcpP and VtrC/ToxS/TcpH have the same cellular localization and membrane topology.
source: Second, VtrA/ToxR/TcpP and VtrC/ToxS/TcpH have the same cellular localization and membrane topology (Miller et al., 1989; Häse and Mekalanos, 1998; Miller et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1989; Häse and Mekalanos, 1998; Miller et al., 1987.

claim: VtrC, ToxS and TcpH affect the activity of VtrA, ToxR and TcpP, respectively.
source: Third, VtrC, ToxS and TcpH affect the activity of VtrA, ToxR and TcpP, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and established knowledge.

claim: VtrA and VtrC form a complex in vivo both before and after T3SS2 activation and in vitro through their periplasmic domains.
source: On this last point, we showed that VtrA and VtrC form a complex in vivo both before and after T3SS2 activation and in vitro through their periplasmic domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro binding data.

claim: Upon binding bile salts to the hydrophobic chamber in the VtrA/VtrC complex, the cytoplasmic DNA binding domain of VtrA is activated and in turn induces VtrB to activate the T3SS2.
source: Our data supports a model in which VtrA and VtrC form a complex both in the absence and presence of bile salts. Upon binding bile salts to the hydrophobic chamber in the VtrA/VtrC complex, the cytoplasmic DNA binding domain of VtrA is activated and in turn induces VtrB to activate the T3SS2 (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is a model inferred from the experimental data and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Bile salts may increase VtrA activity by inducing its dimerization or oligomerization, similar to what has been proposed for the ToxR/ToxS and TcpP/TcpH systems.
source: Although VtrA contains no cysteine residues in its periplasmic domain, it is still possible that bile salts increase VtrA activity by inducing its dimerization or oligomerization, similar to what has been proposed for the ToxR/ToxS and TcpP/TcpH systems (Ottemann and Mekalanos, 1996; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Ottemann and Mekalanos, 1996 and Yang et al., 2013.

claim: The VtrA/VtrC complex is highly conserved in a group of diverse Vibrionaceae family species, as well as in Moritella marina.
source: The VtrA/VtrC complex is highly conserved in a group of diverse Vibrionaceae family species, as well as in Moritella marina.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis.

claim: The bile salt-induced T3SS in V. cholerae non-O1/O139 strains is necessary for bacterial colonization and the primary cause of disease during infection.
source: While the bile salt-induced T3SS in V. cholerae non-O1/O139 strains is necessary for bacterial colonization and the primary cause of disease during infection (Chaand et al., 2015), the role of T3SS in G. hollisae infection is yet to be characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chaand et al., 2015.

claim: Based on surrounding genes, the bile salt receptor complex may have adapted in other species to bind other hydrophilic ligands.
source: Based on surrounding genes, this bile salt receptor complex may have adapted in other species to bind other hydrophilic ligands.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from genomic context analysis.

claim: In the ten strains that lack a vtrB homolog but possess a vtrA/vtrC pair, the gene downstream of the vtrA/vtrC operon encodes a putative sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase.
source: For example, in the ten strains that lack a vtrB homolog but possess a vtrA/vtrC pair, the gene downstream of the vtrA/vtrC operon encodes a putative sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: Sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase is a hydrolase involved in the metabolism of sphingolipids and is a putative virulence factor.
source: This enzyme is a hydrolase involved in the metabolism of sphingolipids (Goñi and Alonso, 2002) and is a putative virulence factor (Oda et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goñi and Alonso, 2002 and Oda et al., 2012.

claim: The homologues of VtrA/VtrC in bacteria lacking vtrB may function as a sensor for sphingolipids and regulate the induction of the downstream gene that produces sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase.
source: It is tempting to hypothesize that the homologues of VtrA/VtrC in these bacteria function as a sensor for sphingolipids and regulate the induction of the downstream gene that produces sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from genomic context.

claim: This study provides the first biochemical and structural analysis of a prokaryotic receptor involved in mediating a response to bile salts.
source: To our knowledge, our study provides the first biochemical and structural analysis of a prokaryotic receptor involved in mediating a response to bile salts, a significant environmental cue during infection.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement of the study's contribution.
